newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey expects 2 billion kWh power deficit in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Turkey expects 2 billion kWh power deficit in 1997.

text.p: Turkey, facing a growing challenge to keep up with rising energy demand, is expected to have a power deficit of two billion kilowatt hours (kWh) in 1997, according to the general manager of state electricity producer TEAS.

Speaking at a forum on energy problems in Turkey, TEAS's Afif Demirkiran said electricity production this year is forecast to reach 103.6 billion kWh, with new capacity amounting to 647 MegaWatts (MW).

He said extensive investment was necessary to keep up with the needs of the Turkish industry. "We cannot meet the demands. By the year 2020 an investment of $99 billion is necessary, excluding transmission facilities and modernisation," he said.
The rise in domestic energy demand in 1996 amounted to 12 percent compared with an expected eight percent, energy ministry official Mehmet Koyuncu told the forum.

Electric power production in 1996 rose by 10.5 percent to 95.4 billion kWh compared with consumption of around 97.5 billion kWh. Turkey began power imports from Iran and Bulgaria late last year to make up the shortfall.
Koyuncu said an annual investment of $2 billion necessary to meet the sharp increase in demand could not be met by the state alone and required private sector initiatives.
The head of Turkey's DSI water authority Dogan Altinbilek said investment of $1 billion was necessary to maximise hydroelectric energy capacity alone.
As part of its efforts to increase energy production, Turkey has also launched a tender for its first nuclear power station.

Energy Minister Recai Kutan told the same forum that 33 lignite and coal-fired power plants, 20 natural gas-fired plants, six thermal, two nuclear and 75 hydroelectric plants had to be made operational in Turkey by 2010 to provide an additional 38,619 MW capacity.
